newsitem.title: JAPAN: Recovery still a tall order for Japanese builders.
newsitem.headline: Recovery still a tall order for Japanese builders.

text.p: Japan's leading construction firms, major casualties of the nation's bad-loan crisis, unveiled a lacklustre set of annual earnings on Monday and predicted another tough year ahead.

The sluggish pace of Japan's economic recovery, coupled with lingering loan woes and a squeeze on public works spending, is putting heavy pressure on builders' earnings and has left any substantial recovery looking elusive.
Among the big four firms, Shimizu Corp and Obayashi Corp suffered lower parent profits in the year to March 1997 and saw their profit slipping further in the current business year.
Kajima Corp posted a higher profit in 1996/97, but predicted a slide this year, while Taisei Corp posted a scant rise in its profits last year and saw earnings only edging up this year.

With Japan's slow recovery putting a tight lid on growth in construction orders from the private sector, analysts warned that it will be some years before construction firms enjoy a full business recovery.

"Our business environment was severe last year, as private construction stayed at low levels...coupled with rapid falls in public-sector construction," industry leader Shimizu Corp said in a statement.

Shimizu's parent current profit slid to 25.58 billion yen ($220 million) last business year from 25.78 billion yen ($222 million). It saw profit sliding down further to 25 billion yen ($215 million) this year.
Shimizu saw more pain ahead due to falling public construction, a slowdown in construction of apartments and sluggishness in the market for office buildings.

Obayashi announced on Monday that its parent current profit fell three percent to 29.42 billion yen ($253 million) in 1996/97, and saw profits sliding again to 29 billion yen ($250 million) in 1997/98.

Profits at Kajima, meanwhile, grew nine percent to 25.06 billion yen ($216 million) in 1996/97, but the firm predicted a 12.2 percent fall this year. Taisei's current profit grew 2.8 percent to 26.11 billion yen ($225 million) last business year and the firm predicted a rise of 3.4 percent this year.

The construction sector has been struggling to recover from the collapse of Japan's 1980s "bubble" of sky-high asset prices, which left them heavily encumbered with problem loans. Builders led the bubble-era investment in property and real estate and also guaranteed loans by their real estate units.

Many firms are still suffering asset quality problems. The amount of debts guaranteed by 98 leading Japanese builders stood at 3.22 trillion yen ($27.7 billion) at the end of September, according to credit research firm Teikoku Databank Ltd.

Japan's frustratingly slow recovery from the post-bubble slump is likely to keep manufacturers and other Japanese firms from planning large capital spending, delaying a substantial turnaround in the construction sector, analysts said.

"I could not detect any major improvement in private-sector construction orders last business year, and they are expected to move sideways this year," said an analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.
"Since the orders move ahead of construction firms' business, their business recovery may not come until the next business year or the year after next," he said.

Credit rating firm Moody's Investors Service said in a report late last month that the prolonged weakness of Japan's private construction market and an expected slowdown in public works spending would hamper the construction sector's business recovery.
Moody's also said efforts by the Japanese government to cut costs would restrain profit margins at contractors in an increasingly competitive market.

A Japanese newspaper reported on Monday that the government would set a target of trimming the nation's public works spending by more than 15 percent over the three years from April 1, 1998. ($1=116 yen)
